findings.source_passage: he said he would go with him to see what madmen there were in the house; so they went upstairs, and with them some of those who were present. Approaching a cage in which there was a furious madman, though just at that moment calm and quiet
findings.source_locator: madhouse story, approach to the cage
findings.why_it_matters: The spatial staging—upstairs, the cage, the furious madman 'just at that moment calm and quiet'—gives the scene its theatrical and ironic texture; the draft collapses this into a bare summary, losing the carefully constructed visual irony.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the upstairs procession, the cage detail, and the parenthetical 'though just at that moment calm and quiet' to preserve the scene's dramatic staging.

findings.source_passage: 'I know I am cured,' returned the licentiate, 'and that I shall not have to go stations again.'
findings.source_locator: madhouse dialogue, after the naked madman's first challenge
findings.why_it_matters: This brief exchange—especially 'go stations again'—is a distinctive colloquial idiom that anchors the licentiate's voice and the ironic comedy of the scene; its absence flattens a key moment in the dialogue.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the licentiate's reply verbatim, including the idiomatic 'go stations again.'

findings.source_passage: it seems to me thou art precipitating thyself from the height of thy madness into the profound abyss of thy simplicity
findings.source_locator: curate's aside to himself, after Don Quixote's offer of advice to the king
findings.why_it_matters: This aside is one of the rhetorically sharpest lines in the chapter—a layered irony about the relationship between madness and simplicity. The draft preserves it verbatim, but buries it mid-paragraph without the theatrical separation ('said to himself') that gives it punch.
findings.suggested_fix: Set the curate's aside off as its own sentence or short paragraph to restore its rhetorical isolation and dramatic weight.

findings.source_passage: he was a graduate of Osuna in canon law; but even if he had been of Salamanca, it was the opinion of most people that he would have been mad all the same
findings.source_locator: barber's madhouse story, opening description of the licentiate
findings.why_it_matters: The Osuna/Salamanca joke is a signature piece of Cervantine academic satire; its absence removes a layer of period-specific irony that has attracted critical comment.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the parenthetical joke about Salamanca when introducing the graduate.

findings.source_passage: no one now, issuing from the wood, penetrates yonder mountains, and then treads the barren, lonely shore of the sea
findings.source_locator: Don Quixote's lament for chivalry, the 'little bark' passage
findings.why_it_matters: The source has 'issuing from the wood, penetrates yonder mountains, and then treads'—a three-beat spatial movement; the draft omits the mountains entirely, weakening the rhetorical climax of the peripatetic image.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'penetrates yonder mountains, and then treads' to preserve the three-stage journey that gives the sentence its cumulative force.

summary: The draft is broadly faithful and preserves all high-priority signatures, but suffers several medium-level voice flattenings—chiefly in the madhouse scene's staging and dialogue—and a handful of minor omissions; none rises to regeneration threshold.
